description: we’re building a web game where players plan a mission to the Moon or Mars, build a spacecraft and pick a rocket on a limited budget, then see if their choices lead to success.
summary:
"Roket Geprek" is a cooperative educational game that teaches students how to design and execute space missions. Players work together in real-time, taking on two distinct roles: the Navigator (managing trajectory and engines) and the Specialist (operating spacecraft instruments). Together, they assemble a spacecraft while navigating real world constraints, such as : mass, power, fuel, and budget for complete missions inspired by actual NASA endeavors, including CubeSat projects and the Artemis II mission.

The game offers an interactive approach to learning about space missions. Instead of memorizing complex physics formulas, students explore orbital mechanics through hands-on, cause-and-effect experimentation, guided by the mascot "Pok-Pok."

Designed as a lightweight, browser-based game, it requires no installation or user account, ensuring smooth performance on both mobile phones and low-specification laptops. This accessibility is crucial for fostering an interest in STEM among the younger generation.

Furthermore, the game bridges global space exploration with local context. Like as highlighting initiatives such as the rocket launch project in Biak, Papua. Thereby inspiring the next generation of space mission designers from Indonesia.
details:
Roket Geprek is a cooperative game that teaches how space missions are designed and flown. Players build a spacecraft within real constraints (mass, power, fuel, slots, and budget) and then fly the mission themselves. Every design choice matters in flight: an underpowered spacecraft runs out of battery, an overweight one fails at launch, and too little fuel means no way to land.

There are four missions, each inspired by a real one:

1. CubeSat Transmission: launch a CubeSat from Biak, Papua, deploy it safely in low Earth orbit, and send its first signal to the BRIN ground station.

2. Around the Moon: fly a free-return trajectory like Artemis II, make mid-course corrections, and hit the narrow re-entry corridor.

3. Lunar South Pole: brake from lunar orbit, land upright without an atmosphere, then manage power in long polar shadows to scan for water ice and send data to Earth.

4. Landing on Mars: protect the instruments from solar storms, program the entry angle, parachute, and landing rockets, then watch the “seven minutes of terror” play out with no way to intervene.

Our game is played by two players in the same room, connecting via a four-letter code entered on their respective devices. Each player has a distinct role: the Navigator manages the physics simulation, controlling throttle, trajectory, and engine ignition timing. The Specialist operates the spacecraft deploying solar panels, orienting antennas, capturing images, running onboard instruments, and monitoring predicted flight paths. The Specialist’s interface allows for sending commands and receiving live updates via a real-time database. Both players must coordinate closely, much like a real-life mission control team.

Our mascot "Pok-Pok", provides step-by-step guidance for beginners, while experienced players can disable these assists to take full manual control. Following each mission, an evaluation is provided, explaining the outcome in accessible, easy to understand language. Missions completed efficiently earn additional funding, which can be added to the budget for subsequent missions.

Inspiration from actual NASA missions, ranging from the development of CubeSats to the Artemis II launch at 2025. We want to make space mission design feel approachable and exciting for students, especially in Indonesia, where hands-on space education is rare. We hope teachers can use Roket Geprek in classrooms, and that players finish a session understanding why real missions are planned the way they are, and maybe wanting to build one someday. The two-role design rewards clear communication under time pressure. It runs in any modern browser on laptops and phones, with no installation and no account, plus a lighter 2D mode for older devices.

players discover orbital mechanics (gravity turns, orbital speed, free-return trajectories, re-entry corridors, powered landings) by experiencing cause and effect, not by memorizing formulas. The Build screen shows that every gram, watt, and dollar is a trade-off, which is the core of real mission design. Missions launch from Biak and use Indonesia’s BRIN ground station, connecting global space exploration to Indonesian students.

Design is our original illustrations, UI, and the Pok-Pok mascot created by our design team.

This game is a web browser based. Its build with JavaScript (ES modules), HTML, and CSS, built with Vite. Graphics using Three.js for 3D planets and spacecraft, with an HTML Canvas 2D fallback. For Multiplayer share using Firebase Realtime Database for rooms and live sync. code was developed with help from an AI coding assistant (Claude Code). The game concept, mission design, data, and art were created by the team. Standard laptops and smartphones for development and testing. No special hardware is required to play.
